title: Does my NSW food business need a food safety supervisor, and how long does the certificate last?
description: NSW Food Authority FSS rules: which businesses need one per premises, the approved units and key focus areas, the 5 year certificate and recertification.
shortAnswer: In New South Wales, every retail, hospitality and food service business that prepares and serves ready to eat, potentially hazardous food not sold in the supplier's original package must appoint at least one Food Safety Supervisor (FSS) per premises. The FSS must hold an NSW Food Authority FSS certificate from an approved Registered Training Organisation, a copy must be kept on the premises, and the certificate must be renewed every five years.
keyTakeaways: At least one FSS is required per premises for businesses serving ready to eat, potentially hazardous food that is not in the supplier's original package; businesses licensed by the NSW Food Authority do not need one.
An FSS cannot be the FSS for any other premises or mobile catering business, and must be able to train and supervise others, citing section 106B of the Food Act 2003 (NSW).
The NSW certificate requires approved national units (SITXFSA005 and SITXFSA006 for hospitality, or SIRRFSA001 for retail) plus four NSW key focus areas.
Certificates expire five years from issue; recertification courses are available only up to 90 days after expiry, after which the full course must be repeated.
A copy of the FSS certificate must be kept on the premises, and RTOs may charge no more than $30 to issue it.
jurisdiction: Australia (New South Wales): Food Act 2003 (NSW), Food Regulation and Food Standards Code Standard 3.2.2A
regulator: NSW Food Authority, with local councils inspecting retail and hospitality businesses
appliesTo: Cafes, restaurants, quick service venues, takeaway shops and caterers
Pubs and clubs with food service areas, motels, mobile vendors and home based food businesses
Supermarkets, delicatessens and greengrocers selling potentially hazardous ready to eat food
School canteens, children's services providing meals, boarding schools and correctional centers
Outlets selling food through third party ordering apps

sections.heading: Which NSW businesses must appoint a food safety supervisor?

blocks.text: All retail, hospitality and food service businesses in NSW must appoint at least one FSS per premises if the food they prepare and serve is ready to eat, potentially hazardous (needs temperature control), and not sold and served in the supplier's original package. The [NSW Food Authority](https://www.foodauthority.nsw.gov.au/retail/fss-food-safety-supervisors) describes this broadly as every business selling potentially hazardous food to the public that is not licensed by the Food Authority.

The Food Authority's list goes well beyond restaurants. It names pubs and clubs with food service areas, mobile vendors, home based businesses, motels, supermarkets selling items such as hot chickens, outlets selling through third party ordering apps, school canteens, children's services including out of school hours care, coffee vendors selling unpackaged ready to eat food, boarding schools and correctional centers.

The NSW program sits alongside the national requirement in Standard 3.2.2A, which applies to category one and category two businesses across Australia. The national rules are covered on the [Standard 3.2.2A training](/regulations/food-safety-standard-3-2-2a-training) page; this page covers what New South Wales adds on top, including approved units, key focus areas and certificate administration.

sections.heading: Which food businesses are exempt in NSW?

blocks.text: Five groups are exempt from the NSW FSS requirement. Businesses outside these groups that handle unpackaged, potentially hazardous, ready to eat food should assume they need an FSS.

items: Handling or selling food solely to raise funds for community or charitable causes, or providing food free to the community.
Businesses licensed with the NSW Food Authority, which are covered by other food safety arrangements.
Businesses that only manufacture or wholesale food with no direct sale to consumers.
Coffee vans that only heat milk for hot drinks and do not handle unpackaged, potentially hazardous food.
Businesses not serving or selling unpackaged food that is potentially hazardous and ready to eat, such as a convenience store selling food only in its original sealed packaging.

sections.heading: Who can be the food safety supervisor?

blocks.text: The business owner nominates the FSS, who may be the owner, a manager or an employee such as the chef. The person must not be the FSS for any other food premises or mobile catering business, must be able to train and supervise others to ensure safe food handling, and must be reasonably available and easily contacted, for example by phone.

blocks.title: Primary text: NSW Food Authority
blocks.text: "Larger businesses that operate longer hours may choose to nominate several people to be trained and appointed as an FSS to help cover shift work and annual leave."

The one premises restriction is the rule multi site operators most often miss. An area manager cannot hold the FSS role for five outlets; each outlet needs its own nominated person. Rosters should show an FSS, or a trained deputy who is also certified, across trading hours.

sections.heading: What training leads to an NSW FSS certificate?

blocks.text: The FSS must complete approved national units of competency plus NSW key focus areas with a single RTO approved for the NSW FSS program. There are two pathways: hospitality, for businesses where food is typically prepared and eaten on site, and retail, for businesses that provide food as a product eaten elsewhere.

blocks.caption: Units and key focus areas accepted for the NSW FSS certificate (as at November 2026)
head: Component
Hospitality pathway
Retail pathway
rows: SITXFSA005 Use hygiene practices for food safety, and SITXFSA006 Participate in safe food handling practices
SIRRFSA001 Handle food safely in a retail environment
Allergen management; cleaning and sanitizing practices; safe egg handling; Food Act offenses
Face to face, online, workplace based, correspondence or a mix; often one full day face to face

blocks.text: The Food Authority notes that the training does not provide all the skills needed to supervise food handling in specific licensed industries such as aged care or manufacturing, and that previous units of competency remain valid until the expiry date on an existing certificate.

sections.heading: How long is an NSW FSS certificate valid?

blocks.text: Five years from the date of issue. The Food Authority states that the Food Act 2003 requires FSS certificates to be renewed every five years, and RTOs must issue the certificate within 10 working days of successful completion.

When a certificate expires, the business has 30 days to either have the person complete a recertification course or appoint another eligible staff member with a current certificate. Recertification courses are offered only to existing NSW FSS holders and only up to 90 days after the previous certificate's expiry; after that the full course must be completed again. Expired certificates cannot be reprinted, replaced or renewed.

The Food Authority will also issue an FSS certificate to someone who completed all required units with a single Australian RTO as part of a vocational qualification, such as a Certificate IV in Commercial Cookery, no more than 6 months before the request. This is a narrow form of [recognition of prior learning](/glossary/recognition-of-prior-learning).

sections.heading: What should an NSW food business keep as evidence?

blocks.text: A business should be able to show a current certificate on the premises for each nominated FSS and a plan for renewal before expiry. The table maps each NSW obligation to role, frequency and evidence; it is illustrative, not a Food Authority form.

head: Obligation
Role

Evidence an inspector would expect
rows: Appoint at least one FSS per premises

Within 30 days of expiry; recertification course only within 90 days
Recertification certificate, or new FSS appointment record
Induction and refresher records for food handlers; supervisor sign off
Roster showing FSS or certified deputy on shift or contactable

blocks.text: Recording expiry dates in a [training matrix](/glossary/training-matrix) with an alert 60 to 90 days ahead keeps the business out of the 30 day replacement window. See also [how to prepare training records for an audit](/guides/how-to-prepare-training-records-for-an-audit). Licensed venues should track FSS dates next to [NSW RSA competency cards](/regulations/responsible-service-of-alcohol-training-nsw), which follow a separate five year cycle.

sections.heading: How does Knowledge Foundry approach this?

blocks.text: Knowledge Foundry maps the four NSW key focus areas and each site's food handling procedures to defined outcomes and assessment points, so the FSS's duty to train other handlers produces evidence, not just attendance. Certificate expiry is held as a competence requirement per premises. See [operational procedure programs](/programs/operational-procedures).

faqs.q: Can one person be the food safety supervisor for two NSW cafes?
faqs.a: No. The NSW Food Authority says the FSS must not be the FSS for any other food premises or mobile catering business. Each premises needs its own nominated FSS, and larger businesses can nominate several certified people at one premises to cover shifts and leave.

faqs.q: Does an NSW FSS certificate from years ago still count?
faqs.a: Only if it was issued within the last five years. Certificates expire five years from issue. A recertification course is available up to 90 days after expiry; beyond that, the full course must be completed again, and expired certificates cannot be reprinted or renewed.

faqs.q: Do food handlers other than the FSS need training in NSW?
faqs.a: Yes, under the national Standard 3.2.2A, food handlers in category one and two businesses must complete a food safety training course or have equivalent skills and knowledge. The FSS requirement adds a certified supervisor; it does not replace handler training.

faqs.q: How much can an RTO charge for the NSW FSS certificate?
faqs.a: The NSW Food Authority says RTOs may charge only $30 to issue the NSW FSS certificate itself. Course fees are separate and set by each RTO, as are fees for reissuing a lost or damaged certificate.

factCheck.claim: All retail, hospitality and food service businesses must appoint at least one FSS per premises if food is ready to eat, potentially hazardous, and not sold in the supplier's original package; Food Authority licensed businesses do not need an FSS; list of covered business types.

FSS must not be FSS for any other premises or mobile catering business and must be able to train and supervise others (Food Act 2003 s106B(1c) as cited by the Food Authority); must be reasonably available.
Accepted units: SITXFSA005 and SITXFSA006 (hospitality) or SIRRFSA001 (retail); key focus areas: allergen management, cleaning and sanitising, safe egg handling, Food Act offences.
Food Act 2003 requires certificates renewed every 5 years; RTOs issue within 10 working days; certificate fee capped at $30; copy must be kept on premises.

On expiry, business has 30 days to recertify the FSS or appoint another; recertification only up to 90 days after expiry; expired certificates cannot be reprinted or renewed; RPL for units from a vocational qualification within 6 months.

Exemptions: charitable fundraising and free food, Food Authority licensed businesses, manufacture or wholesale only, coffee vans only heating milk, businesses not selling unpackaged potentially hazardous ready to eat food.
